title: Refactor this if/else chain
summary: The live-refactor skill: recognize the axis of variation, apply the smallest pattern that fits, and say when you'd stop.

slides.markdown:
"Refactor this if/else chain" usually comes as a live-coding exercise: you're handed a function with a growing chain of `if/else` or `switch` branches and asked to clean it up on the spot. It's testing whether you can recognize *what's varying* under time pressure and apply the smallest pattern that actually fits — not whether you can recite every refactoring technique in a book.

The skill is triage: diagnose fast, refactor incrementally, and don't over-apply a pattern just because you have one ready.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying question: is the chain branching on type, on state, or on a config flag?
slides.markdown:
Ask this before touching any code, since it changes the target shape. Branching on **type** (`if (shape instanceof Circle)`) usually resolves to polymorphic dispatch or Factory. Branching on **state** (`if (order.status == SHIPPED)`) points at State. Branching on a **config flag** (`if (featureFlag)`) is often better left as a conditional, or handled by a feature-flag-aware Strategy if the branches are genuinely complex.

Naming which one you're looking at before proposing a fix shows structured thinking under interview time pressure.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: name the axis, name the smallest pattern that fits, don't over-apply
slides.markdown:
The answer skeleton: name the axis the chain branches on, name the smallest pattern that fits that axis, then say explicitly that you wouldn't over-apply it. "This branches on type, so I'd move toward polymorphic dispatch — but I'd only introduce a full Strategy hierarchy if the branches are complex enough to warrant separate classes; a lookup map of lambdas might be enough."

Stating the "don't over-apply" clause out loud, unprompted, is what separates a strong live-refactor answer from a mechanical one.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: the original if/else chain branching on a type field
Code: step one — extract each branch into its own method
Code: step two — replace the chain with polymorphic dispatch or a lookup map of Strategy objects
Diagram: the refactor as three steps — extract, classify, replace
slides.markdown:
![Three-step refactor flow: extract each branch into a method, classify what varies, then replace with the matching pattern](assets/refactor-three-steps.svg)

Doing the steps in this order — extract before you classify, classify before you replace — keeps every intermediate state compiling and testable, which matters enormously when you're refactoring live in front of someone.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a lookup map of lambdas vs a full Strategy class hierarchy — when each is enough
slides.markdown:
| | Lookup map of lambdas | Full Strategy class hierarchy |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Branches that are one-liners or simple expressions | Branches with real logic, state, or shared setup |
| Boilerplate | Minimal — a `Map` literal | One interface plus one class per variant |
| Testability | Harder to unit test a lambda in isolation | Each strategy class is independently testable |
| Discoverability | Implementation lives inline, less discoverable | Each variant is a named, findable class |

**How to decide:** if a branch is more than a couple of lines or needs its own dependencies, promote it to a real class; if every branch is a one-liner, the lookup map is less ceremony for the same result.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "what if the branches share 80% of their logic?" — template method pulls the shared part up
slides.markdown:
When branches share most of their logic and differ in only one step, Strategy stops being the best fit — extracting the whole branch into a separate class duplicates the 80% that's identical across all of them. [Template Method](iv-template-method-vs-strategy) is the better shape here: put the shared steps in a base class or a single method, and let only the one varying step be overridden or injected per branch.

Recognizing "mostly shared, one step different" as a distinct case from "entirely different per branch" is exactly the judgment call this follow-up is checking for.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "how do you do this live without breaking existing tests mid-refactor?"
slides.markdown:
Run the existing test suite before touching anything, so you have a known-green baseline. Then refactor in the smallest steps that keep it green: extract methods first (tests still pass, behavior literally unchanged), then introduce the pattern (tests still pass, since the extracted methods' bodies didn't change, just how they're dispatched to).

Narrating this out loud — "I'll extract first and re-run tests before I touch dispatch" — during a live exercise shows disciplined process, which often matters as much as the final code shape.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: refactoring correctly but never naming the pattern you landed on
slides.markdown:
**Weak belief:** doing the whole refactor correctly — extracting methods, moving to a lookup map — without ever saying "this is Strategy" out loud.

**Why it's weak:** the interviewer is also checking pattern vocabulary, not just code quality; silently landing on the right shape without naming it leaves the interviewer to infer whether you did it on purpose or by accident.

**Correct model:** narrate the pattern as you land on it — "I've turned this into a lookup-map version of Strategy" — so there's no ambiguity about whether the shape was deliberate.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: replacing a two-branch if/else that will never grow with a full Strategy hierarchy
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** turning every `if/else` you're handed into a full Strategy class hierarchy, regardless of how many branches it has or whether it will ever grow.

**Why it's wrong:** a two-branch conditional with no indication it'll ever need a third branch doesn't need an interface and two classes — that's more code, more files, and more indirection for zero actual flexibility gained, and it signals you refactor by reflex rather than by judgment.

**Correct model:** state the threshold explicitly during the exercise — "if this stays at two branches, I'd leave it as a conditional; I'd only introduce Strategy once it's three or more, or callers need to swap behavior at runtime."

Extract each branch into its own method first — reversible, testable, no pattern yet. Classify what the branches vary on: type points at polymorphism, state points at State, a config flag might stay a conditional. Replace with the smallest fitting shape — often a lookup map of lambdas beats a full class hierarchy when branches are simple.

Narrate the pattern you land on, name the threshold where you'd stop refactoring, and re-run tests after each step rather than at the very end.
